title: How to Teach (with AI)
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles demonstrates how he used Google's NotebookLM, restricted to four trusted sources (Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, Robert Coe's What Makes Great Teaching, an NSW cognitive load theory guide, and the APA's Top 20 Principles), to generate a three-lesson sequence on the Inspector in An Inspector Calls. He shows the resulting worked examples and scaffolded, partially-completed practice tasks, noting that NotebookLM's grounding in trusted sources keeps its output evidence-aligned and that its citations link directly back to the relevant passage in the source material. Salles argues teachers retain the professional judgement to adjust tone or reading level, but that uploading a small set of high-quality pedagogical sources turns NotebookLM into a generator of classroom-ready lesson sequences, worked examples, and scaffolded practice tasks for any topic or subject.
points: Salles' method is the piece's transferable core: restricting NotebookLM to a small set of trusted pedagogical sources (Rosenshine, Coe, cognitive load theory, APA's Top 20) rather than the open internet, so its output stays evidence-aligned rather than generic.

His worked-example outputs follow an explicit "I Do, We Do, You Do" structure with scaffolds and partially completed problems, directly reflecting the guided-practice principles drawn from his four source documents.

The clickable-citation feature (each generated claim links back to the exact passage in the uploaded source) is presented as a meaningful trust mechanism, distinct from an ordinary chatbot's unverifiable output.

Salles is explicit that professional judgement still matters -- flagging that one generated worked example was pitched at too high a reading level for most classrooms -- positioning AI as a generator of raw material, not a replacement for teacher review.
quotes: AI hallucinates. It’s cheating. It stops teachers thinking for themselves. It’s never going to be as good as my professional expertise. All these statements might be true.
NotebookLM is an AI which will only use the sources which you trust. You can upload up to 50 such sources - PDFs, webpages, YouTube videos.
This would mean whatever activities it generated for my students would be high value, with a direct impact on learning.

The lesson structure adheres to principles like beginning with a review of previous learning, presenting new material in small steps with practice after each step, providing models, and guiding practice.
This language is a bit academic for most classrooms - this is where your professional judgement comes in.
Uploading these 4 sources to NotebookLM will give you dozens of high quality ideas for you to steal and adapt.
